name: Niacinamide
lead: Niacinamide, also called nicotinamide, is the amide form of vitamin B3. It is found in foods such as yeast, meat, milk and green vegetables, is sold as a dietary supplement and medication, and is incorporated into cosmetic serums, moisturizers and cleansers.[1] Within cells it is a precursor of the coenzymes NAD+ and NADP+, which take part in many oxidation-reduction reactions.[1] Unlike nicotinic acid (niacin), it does not cause skin flushing at ordinary doses.[1] Many serums and moisturizers pair it with other actives, and it is one of the most common ingredients in everyday skin-care routines.

In skin care it is promoted for improving barrier function, reducing sebum, evening skin tone and calming redness.[2][3] Reviews describe antipruritic, antimicrobial, vasoactive, photoprotective, sebostatic and lightening effects that depend on concentration and on how well the compound is delivered into skin.[3][5] A 2025 Delphi consensus of 62 dermatologists included niacinamide among the ingredients cosmetic dermatologists frequently recommend, for redness and dark spots.[4]

Published human trials of topical niacinamide are mostly small, often industry-linked, and use short treatment periods; one 2014 review noted that existing data were not sufficient for a scientifically founded evaluation of its therapeutic use even while describing the prospects as interesting.[3] A 2026 review concluded that topical nicotinamide has the most developed clinical evidence for wrinkles, texture, pigmentation and barrier function, while calling for longer skin-focused trials.[27] Outside cosmetics, oral nicotinamide is the standard treatment for pellagra,[1][25] has reduced new non-melanoma skin cancers in a phase 3 trial of high-risk adults,[26] and has been studied for glaucoma.[1]

paras: Topical niacinamide is marketed for oil control and pore appearance, barrier support, redness, uneven tone and signs of ageing.[2][3] The 2025 dermatologist consensus assigned it to redness and dark spots.[4] A review on dermal delivery describes brightening, anti-ageing and barrier-protective roles.[2]

Oral nicotinamide is the preferred treatment for pellagra, the niacin deficiency disease, because it avoids niacin's flushing.[1] Wikipedia reports that nicotinamide cream is used for acne, that oral doses of 500 to 1000 mg daily reduced the risk of non-melanoma skin cancers in people at high risk, and that it is under investigation for glaucoma but is not approved for that use.[1] Reviews also cover topical use in dermatitis, acne vulgaris and actinic keratosis.[2]

Evidence is described as most developed for skin tone, barrier function and sebum. In a 2002 British Journal of Dermatology study, niacinamide reduced melanin transfer in laboratory models, and in clinical portions a 5 percent niacinamide moisturizer was compared with vehicle in 18 subjects with hyperpigmentation, and 2 percent niacinamide with sunscreen was tested in 120 subjects with facial tanning.[7] A 2005 randomized trial in 50 white female subjects assessed effects on wrinkles, yellowing and elasticity in ageing facial skin, building on earlier studies reporting improvements in hyperpigmented spots and red blotchiness.[6] A 2006 randomized trial examined 2 percent niacinamide and facial sebum production.[8]

Wikipedia summarises that 2 percent topical nicotinamide applied for two to four weeks lowered the sebum excretion rate, and that in vitro it raises ceramide synthesis in keratinocytes.[1] Reviews caution that results depend on formulation and skin penetration.[2] The dermatologist consensus noted that most consensus ingredients were supported by level 1b or 2b evidence while some rested on expert opinion.[4]

Randomized and controlled trials of topical niacinamide have examined skin pigmentation and tanning (the 2002 study of Japanese women, with 18- and 120-subject arms),[7] ageing facial skin in 50 female subjects (2005),[6] sebum production with 2 percent niacinamide (2006),[8] and acne, including a 2024 split-face randomized trial of a ceramide and niacinamide moisturizer added to anti-acne treatment.[11] A 2025 randomized double-blind trial compared niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone in melasma,[9] and a 2021 randomized trial of scalp antioxidant application assessed shedding over 24 weeks.[10] A 2023 randomized study evaluated niacinamide body emollients in mild atopic dermatitis.[12]

Registered trials include a planned comparison of topical vitamin C and niacinamide for melasma (n=100, not yet recruiting) and studies of oral nicotinamide in glaucoma (n=58), kidney conditions, ataxia telangiectasia and cardiac surgery injury.[13][14][15] Reviews of the literature are available on mechanisms, clinical evidence and delivery strategies.[2][3][5][12]

Reviews describe topical niacinamide as well tolerated and safe.[3] Occasional flushing, itching or irritation has been reported with higher concentrations or particular formulations.[2] For oral use, Wikipedia reports minimal side effects, liver problems at high doses (acute liver toxicity documented in at least one case above 3,000 mg per day), a contraindication in liver disease, and safety at normal amounts in pregnancy.[1] A US antiperspirant label containing niacinamide advises consulting a doctor before use in people with kidney disease, although that warning concerns the product rather than the ingredient alone.[16]

In cells nicotinamide is converted via a salvage pathway into NAD+ and NADP+.[1] Pharmacological reviews describe inhibition of the enzyme PARP-1 and effects on NF-kappaB-mediated transcription of signalling molecules.[3] Laboratory work reports suppressed transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes,[7] increased ceramide synthesis,[1] and reduced Cutibacterium acnes-induced activation of toll-like receptor 2 with lower interleukin-8 production.[1]

Nicotinamide consists of a pyridine ring with a primary amide at the 3 position and is the amide of nicotinic acid. Industrially it is produced enzymatically from nicotinonitrile; Wikipedia gives a worldwide sales figure of 31,000 tons in 2014.[1]

Wikipedia states that nicotinamide was discovered between 1935 and 1937 and that it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1] The vitamin's story begins with pellagra, a disease first described by the Spanish physician Gaspar Casal in 1735, which became epidemic in the American South in the early twentieth century.[25] Joseph Goldberger linked pellagra to diet in the 1910s and 1920s, and in 1937-1938 Conrad Elvehjem showed that vitamin B3 cured black tongue in dogs, after which Tom Spies and colleagues showed it cured pellagra in people.[25] Food fortification with niacin followed, and pellagra was largely eliminated in the United States by the 1950s.[25]

Nicotinamide is the form with lower toxicity than nicotinic acid and became the standard treatment for pellagra.[25] Its use in cosmetics grew through published trials from the early 2000s, including the 2002 pigmentation study, which has been cited several hundred times.[7] The 2015 phase 3 trial in skin-cancer chemoprevention brought oral nicotinamide into dermatology practice,[26] and a 2023 trial extended the question to transplant recipients.[28]

A double-blind phase 3 trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2015 enrolled 386 people with at least two non-melanoma skin cancers in the previous five years. Participants took oral nicotinamide or placebo for 12 months. The nicotinamide group had a 23 percent lower rate of new non-melanoma skin cancers, with lower rates of actinic keratoses at each check, and adverse events did not differ meaningfully between groups; the benefit did not persist after treatment stopped.[26]

A 2023 New England Journal of Medicine trial examined nicotinamide for chemoprevention in transplant recipients,[28] and a 2026 review describes oral nicotinamide as reducing new squamous cell carcinomas and actinic keratoses during treatment in high-risk patients, while noting heterogeneous evidence.[27] This work concerns oral use in a medical setting and is separate from cosmetic serums.

In routines, niacinamide is used as a leave-on serum or moisturizer ingredient, commonly in the 2 to 5 percent range in the cited trials,[6][7][8] and is often described as a gentle option because, unlike nicotinic acid, it does not cause flushing.[1] People report using it for oiliness, the look of pores, redness, uneven tone and early signs of ageing.[2][3] Reviews say outcomes depend on concentration, formulation and penetration into skin.[2][5]

Studies run in combination, such as ceramide-containing moisturizers added to acne treatment,[11] and trials comparing tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone in melasma,[9] reflect how often it is paired with other actives rather than used alone. Results from combination products cannot be attributed to niacinamide alone, a point reviews of dermocosmetics make about multi-ingredient products generally.[29]

Nicotinic acid (niacin) is the other common form of vitamin B3 and causes flushing, while niacinamide does not; the two have different effects on blood lipids.[1] Other NAD+ precursors are the subject of a growing research literature on ageing and skin.[27] Cosmetic users often combine niacinamide with retinoids, vitamin C, hyaluronic acid or azelaic acid in a single routine; research on these pairings is limited to individual product studies.[2][11]

On T Nation, niacinamide appears mostly as an oral supplement rather than a skin product. Posters list it in stacks for brain function and anxiety, in hormone-related troubleshooting threads, and in cholesterol discussions where one poster states that niacinamide, unlike niacin, does not affect cholesterol.[17][18][19][20][21]

Niacinamide is a staple ingredient of consumer skin-care routines, and claims such as shrinking pores, clearing congestion and brightening are common in product marketing and user discussion.[2] Dermatologists' consensus lists it for redness and dark spots,[4] and reviews describe pore and oil effects as modest and formulation dependent.[2][8]

lore.intro: On T Nation, niacinamide is discussed mostly as an oral supplement in cognitive, mood and hormone-support stacks,[17][20] while in skin-care communities it is discussed as a serum ingredient for oil, pores and tone.[2]

claims.claim: Niacinamide improves anxiety and stress resilience
claims.believers: One poster lists niacinamide 500 mg with theanine and passionflower as things that helped with anxiety and stressful situations.[19]
claims.experts: A 1970 trial of niacinamide in 57 children with schizophrenia found no significant difference from placebo; no trial of niacinamide for anxiety has been published.[22]

claims.claim: Niacinamide supports energy and brain function through NAD+
claims.believers: Supplement lists in brain-booster threads describe niacinamide as important B-complex support, with some users arguing that regular niacin converts to NADH more effectively.[17][18]
claims.experts: Biochemistry confirms that nicotinamide is a precursor of NAD+ through a salvage pathway; the effects of supplementation on cognition in healthy people have not been shown.[1]

claims.claim: Niacinamide helps with hormone or TRT-related symptoms
claims.believers: A poster on a TRT thread suggested trying niacinamide to raise progesterone, and another reported feeling better after adding it before the effect faded.[23][24]
claims.experts: No published human studies test niacinamide for these purposes.

claims.believers: A forum reply says niacin helps HDL while niacinamide 'does nothing for cholesterol'.[21]
claims.experts: Reviews distinguish niacinamide from nicotinic acid, noting for example that nicotinic acid causes flushing and niacinamide does not.[1]

claims.claim: Topical niacinamide reduces oil, redness and dark spots
claims.believers: Skin-care users promote it as a barrier, oil and tone product.[2]
claims.experts: Randomized trials report effects on sebum and pigmentation, and a dermatologist consensus lists it for redness and dark spots, with reviews noting modest effects that vary by formulation.[7][8][4][2]

claims.claim: Niacinamide shrinks pores and controls oil.
claims.believers: Skin-care users promote it as a pore-refining, oil-regulating serum ingredient.[2]
claims.experts: A 2006 randomized trial examined 2 percent niacinamide and facial sebum production,[8] and Wikipedia reports lowered sebum excretion over two to four weeks;[1] reviews note that effects depend on formulation.[2]

claims.claim: Niacinamide fades dark spots and evens skin tone.
claims.believers: Users describe more even tone and fewer dark marks with regular serum use.[2]
claims.experts: A 2002 study reported reduced melanosome transfer and trials in hyperpigmentation and tanning,[7] and a dermatologist consensus lists it for dark spots.[4]

claims.claim: Oral nicotinamide helps prevent skin cancer.
claims.believers: Proponents point to the published trial results as the basis for using it in sun-damaged skin.
claims.experts: A 2015 phase 3 trial reported 23 percent fewer new non-melanoma skin cancers in high-risk adults over 12 months, with no benefit after stopping.[26]
